A flare-up is a sudden, often unexpected outbreak or worsening of something — usually something bad — that happens quickly after a period of calm or control.

To truly understand "flare-up," picture a small fire that is barely burning, almost dying out — and then suddenly, a gust of wind hits it, and the flames shoot up violently for a moment. That sudden, dramatic burst is the "flare." A flare-up is that moment — when something that was quiet, controlled, or suppressed suddenly becomes intense and active again.

This image is the heart of the word. Carry it with you, and every use of "flare-up" will make perfect sense.
The key idea behind every use

Three things are almost always true about a flare-up:

  1. It is sudden. It doesn't creep up slowly over weeks. It happens fast — sometimes overnight or even within hours.
  2. It is usually temporary. A flare-up rises quickly, peaks, and then typically settles or calms down again. It is not a permanent state.
  3. It implies something that was already there. This is crucial. A flare-up is not something brand new appearing out of nowhere. It is something — an illness, a conflict, a feeling — that already existed (perhaps quietly or under control) and has now broken out again with force. This sense of recurrence is what makes "flare-up" unique.

1. Medical flare-up (the most common use today)

Many illnesses — especially chronic (long-term) ones — don't stay the same all the time. A person with arthritis, asthma, eczema, lupus, Crohn's disease, or multiple sclerosis, for example, may have long periods where they feel okay and the disease is manageable. But then, sometimes triggered by stress, cold weather, certain foods, or no obvious reason at all, the symptoms suddenly get much worse. That sudden worsening is called a flare-up.

"My sister has eczema. Most of the time her skin is fine, but she had a bad flare-up last winter — her skin became red, cracked, and intensely itchy for two weeks before it calmed down."

"The doctor said the patient was in remission, but she suffered a flare-up of her lupus after a period of stress."

The disease didn't go away — it was just quiet. Then it became suddenly active and severe again. That period of sudden, intense activity is the flare-up.

2. A flare-up of fire or flames

In its more literal sense, a flare-up refers to a sudden burst of fire or flames, especially when a fire that seemed to be dying or under control suddenly grows bigger and more dangerous.

"The firefighters had nearly contained the blaze when a sudden flare-up caused by strong winds sent them retreating."

"There was a dangerous flare-up in the kitchen when oil spilled onto the open flame."

3. A flare-up of conflict, violence, or tension

In news, politics, and international affairs, a flare-up describes a sudden outbreak of fighting, violence, or serious tension — especially in a region or relationship that had been relatively stable.

"After months of fragile peace, there was a sharp flare-up of violence along the disputed border."

"Diplomatic talks broke down, leading to a flare-up of tensions between the two countries."

Again, the conflict was never fully resolved — it was simmering beneath the surface — and now it has burst out suddenly.

4. A flare-up of emotions or temper

A flare-up can also describe a sudden outburst of a strong emotion, most often anger. It happens quickly, it's intense, but it usually passes.

"There was a brief flare-up of anger between the two players on the field, but the referee stepped in and they quickly calmed down."

"His remark caused an unexpected flare-up of frustration in the room."

A flare-up is almost always negative. You will never hear someone describe a "flare-up of joy" or a "flare-up of generosity." The word is reserved for things that cause trouble, pain, danger, or discomfort — illness, fire, conflict, anger.

A flare-up implies a pattern. You don't usually call the very first time something happens a "flare-up." The word suggests this has happened before — or that the underlying problem has been lurking. If someone gets arthritis for the very first time, that's not a flare-up. But after that, each time it suddenly gets much worse, that's a flare-up.

A flare-up can be triggered. Often, a flare-up is set off by something — cold weather, stress, a provocative remark, a political event. That thing is called a trigger. Sometimes there's no clear trigger at all, and the flare-up just happens on its own.

Learning which words naturally pair with "flare-up" will help you use it correctly and recognize it in reading.

  • "A sudden flare-up" — emphasizes how fast it came
  • "A brief flare-up" — emphasizes it didn't last long
  • "A severe / bad flare-up" — emphasizes how intense it was
  • "A flare-up of [condition/problem]" — a flare-up of asthma, a flare-up of violence, a flare-up of tension
  • "A flare-up between [people]" — a flare-up between the two rivals
  • "Suffer / experience a flare-up" — common in medical contexts: "She experienced a flare-up of her condition."
  • "Trigger a flare-up" — "Stress can trigger a flare-up."
  • "Cause a flare-up" — "The comment caused a flare-up of anger."
  • "Have a flare-up" — very natural in everyday speech: "He's having a flare-up."

These words may seem similar, but they each mean something slightly different:

Outbreak — An "outbreak" often refers to something starting or spreading for the first time (like a disease outbreak), not necessarily a recurrence. A flare-up is always about something that already existed becoming active again.

Eruption — Much more dramatic and forceful. An eruption suggests something explosive — like a volcano. A flare-up is sudden and intense, but not necessarily explosive.

Recurrence — A "recurrence" simply means something has come back. It's neutral and doesn't tell you whether it came back suddenly or slowly, mildly or severely. A flare-up, by contrast, always implies it came back suddenly and with intensity.

Episode — In medical language, an "episode" is similar to a flare-up but more clinical and neutral. It doesn't carry the vivid image of something shooting up suddenly the way "flare-up" does.

Surge — A "surge" means a strong increase in something, but it can be gradual and doesn't imply the thing was previously calm or in check.
A final summary to lock it in

A flare-up is a sudden and intense outbreak of something — a disease, fire, conflict, or emotion — that was previously quiet, controlled, or suppressed. It rises quickly, it's usually temporary, and it always implies that the underlying problem was already there. The word is almost always used for something negative, and it carries a vivid image: a flame that shoots up suddenly, burns intensely for a moment, and then — hopefully — dies back down.
